stages.title: Advanced argumentation
stages.hook: A debater says, "Only a fool would oppose this law." Is that a reason? How would you build a strong case, and answer the best objection to it?
explain: Advanced argumentation goes beyond spotting premises. The Toulmin model describes a practical argument in six parts: a claim; grounds (the evidence); a warrant (the general principle that links grounds to claim); backing (support for the warrant); a qualifier (how strong the claim is, such as "probably"); and a rebuttal (conditions under which the claim fails). Many disputes are really about the warrant, not the facts.

Objections come in kinds. A rebutting defeater gives a reason to think the conclusion is false. An undercutting defeater attacks the link: it says the grounds do not support the claim, even if the claim could still be true. A premise objection denies a ground. Strong rebuttal answers the best version of the other view, a practice called steelmanning, and avoids the straw man.

Burden of proof lies on the person making the claim, and a claim's extraordinary content raises the evidence needed. Arguments can also be evaluated probabilistically: each premise has some probability of truth, and the conclusion is weakened as uncertainties accumulate. Good argument aims at understanding and truth, not only winning.

example.q: "This school should start later, because teenagers sleep better, and better sleep improves learning." Give a Toulmin analysis.
steps: Claim: start later. Grounds: teenagers get more sleep with later starts.
Warrant: more sleep improves learning, and learning is the aim of school.
Qualifier: probably. Rebuttal: unless later finishes stop after-school work.
example.a: Claim, grounds, warrant, qualifier and rebuttal identified; the warrant is the link between sleep and learning.

analogies.city: A council argues for a tram: the grounds are rising traffic, the warrant is that public transport cuts congestion, and the rebuttal is "unless ridership is low".
analogies.sport: A coach claims a new training plan works, citing results; a critic undercuts: the squad was also given new boots.
analogies.tech: A developer claims a rewrite will be faster; the rebuttal is "unless the new code adds hidden costs".

stages.mnemonic: Claim, Grounds, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, Rebuttal: the Toulmin six.
terms: Warrant
The principle that links the grounds to the claim.
Undercutting defeater
An objection that the evidence does not support the claim.
Steelmanning
Answering the strongest version of an opposing view.
Burden of proof
The duty to give support, which rests on the one making the claim.

misc.wrong: To refute an argument you must prove its conclusion false.
misc.right: You can undercut an argument, showing its reasons are weak, without showing the conclusion false.

stages.limits: Argument models like Toulmin's are tools; real debates mix values, evidence and rhetoric in ways no single model captures.

trip.prompt: Match the six parts with an example on the page.

questions.q: In the Toulmin model, what links the grounds to the claim?
o: The warrant
The qualifier
The rebuttal
The backing

questions.q: "The street was wet, but it could have been a hose." This is a...
o: Rebuttal to rain as the only explanation
Warrant that links the grounds to the claim
Backing that supports the warrant itself
Claim that the speaker wants us to accept

questions.q: An undercutting defeater differs from a rebutting defeater because it...
o: Attacks the support, not the conclusion
Proves the conclusion to be false outright
Adds a new premise in favour of the claim
Restates the claim in different words
questions.why: It says the evidence does not show the conclusion.

questions.q: Which is steelmanning?
o: Restating the opposing view in its strongest form before replying
Attacking the speaker's character before replying
Ignoring the objections made against your side
Distorting their view into a weaker version of it
questions.why: It is the opposite of a straw man.

questions.q: Who has the burden of proof in a debate?
o: The one making the claim
The audience, who must decide the matter
Whoever is speaking the loudest in the room
The last speaker to talk in the debate

questions.q: A claim is introduced with "probably". Which part is this?
o: The qualifier
The warrant that connects the evidence to the claim
The backing behind the warrant
The grounds on which the claim rests
questions.why: It signals the strength of the claim.

questions.q: Two people agree on all facts but still disagree about a policy. Where might the disagreement lie?
o: In the warrant or the values behind it
In the grounds only, since the facts are shared
In the date on which the policy begins
In the font used to print the report
questions.why: Warrants link facts to what we should do.

questions.q: An argument has three independent premises, each 90% likely to be true. What is the probability that all three are true? Give a decimal to three places.
Match each Toulmin part to its role.
Explain why answering the strongest version of an opponent's argument is better than the weakest.
questions.model: Answering the strongest version tests my view properly and is fair, so if I still hold it I know it survives the best objection, while beating a weak version proves nothing.

panel.q: A report cites 20 studies supporting a claim, but all 20 were funded by the maker. What kind of objection is this?
o: Questions the independence of the grounds
A deductive proof of the claim, which cannot fail
A steelman of the other side's argument
A warrant that connects the grounds to the claim

panel.q: Why does a chain of five reasonable premises, each 80% likely, give a conclusion less than 80% likely?
panel.model: If the premises are independent and all are needed, their probabilities multiply, so 0.8 to the power 5 is about 0.33, and uncertainty accumulates.

panel.q: Which response best handles an undercutting objection?
o: Show that the evidence does support the claim after all, or find better evidence
Repeat the claim louder so the objector hears it
Attack the objector's character instead of the point
Change the topic to something they cannot challenge

teach.model: The Toulmin model has claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal. Objections can rebut the claim or undercut the support. Steelman the opponent, remember the burden of proof, and note that uncertainty accumulates across premises.

points.ask: How should I answer an opponent?

stages.title: Bayesian reasoning
stages.hook: A test for a rare disease is 90% accurate. You test positive. Does that mean there is a 90% chance you have it?
explain: Bayesian reasoning is a rule for updating beliefs when new evidence arrives. Bayes' theorem: P(H | E) = P(E | H) × P(H) ÷ P(E). Here P(H) is the prior (belief before the evidence), P(E | H) is the likelihood (how probable the evidence is if H is true) and P(H | E) is the posterior (belief afterwards). P(E) = P(E | H) P(H) + P(E | not H) P(not H).

Base rates matter. Suppose 1% of people have a condition, the test detects 90% of true cases (sensitivity) and wrongly flags 10% of healthy people (false positive rate). In 1000 people: 10 have it and 9 test positive; 990 do not, and 99 test positive. So 108 test positive, of whom 9 truly have the condition: P = 9/108 ≈ 8.3%, not 90%. Ignoring the base rate is the base rate fallacy.

The odds form is handy: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio, where the likelihood ratio is P(E | H) ÷ P(E | not H). Strong evidence has a large likelihood ratio, but a low prior can still keep the posterior small. Bayesian thinking also applies to everyday belief: update in proportion to evidence, avoid certainties of 0 or 1, and note that different priors can start people in different places and converge as evidence grows.

example.q: Prior P(H) = 0.2. Evidence is 4 times as likely if H is true as if H is false. Find the posterior.
steps: Prior odds: 0.2 : 0.8 = 1 : 4.
Multiply by the likelihood ratio 4: 4 : 4 = 1 : 1.
Probability = 1 ÷ (1 + 1) = 0.5.

analogies.city: A smoke alarm sounds. Most alarms are false from toast, so the prior of fire matters.
analogies.farm: A test flags a disease in a herd where the disease is rare; most flags are false alarms.
analogies.tech: A spam filter flags an email: how likely it is truly spam depends on how much spam there is.

stages.mnemonic: Prior times likelihood, then divide by everything: that is the Bayes ring.
terms: Prior
Probability of a hypothesis before seeing the new evidence.
Likelihood
Probability of the evidence if the hypothesis is true.
Posterior
Probability of the hypothesis after the evidence.
Base rate
How common something is in the population.

misc.wrong: A 90% accurate test means a positive result is 90% likely to be correct.
misc.right: The chance that a positive is correct depends on the base rate. For rare conditions many positives are false.

stages.limits: Bayesian methods need priors, which can be subjective; scholars debate how to choose them and compare Bayesian and frequentist approaches.

trip.prompt: Work through the medical test example and note the role of the base rate.

questions.q: Prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, false positive rate 10%. What is the probability of the condition given a positive test? Give a decimal to three places.
questions.why: Per 1000 people: 9 true positives and 99 false positives, so 9 ÷ 108 ≈ 0.083.

questions.q: What is the prior?
o: Belief before the new evidence
Belief after the new evidence is taken in
The evidence that you have just found
The test that you ran to get the evidence

questions.q: Why is the base rate important for a positive test?
o: It sets how many positives are false alarms
It changes how accurate the test itself is
It is irrelevant once the test result is known
It makes every test result wrong
questions.why: Rare conditions give many false positives.

questions.q: Prior odds 1:4 for a hypothesis. The evidence has a likelihood ratio of 6. What is the posterior probability? Give a decimal.
Posterior odds equal...
o: Prior odds × likelihood ratio
Prior odds + likelihood ratio, added together
Likelihood ÷ prior odds, divided out
Prior odds ÷ likelihood ratio, divided out
questions.why: This is the odds form of Bayes.

questions.q: A bag holds one fair coin and one two-headed coin. You pick one at random and flip heads. What is P(two-headed)?
Which is the base rate fallacy?
o: Ignoring how common something is when judging a probability
Using a prior belief to judge a new claim
Updating beliefs when new evidence arrives
Multiplying probabilities of separate events

questions.q: Why avoid assigning a prior of exactly 0 to a possibility?
o: No evidence could ever raise it
It makes the arithmetic much harder to do
It is rude to dismiss any idea at all
It always gives an answer of exactly 1

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Share of true cases the test detects

questions.q: Why can two people with different priors disagree at first yet agree after enough evidence?
questions.model: Repeated updating on shared evidence moves both beliefs toward the same value, as the data swamps the effect of the starting priors, provided neither started with a prior of 0 or 1.

panel.q: A town has 1 in 1000 people with a condition. A test has 99% sensitivity and 1% false positive rate. Roughly what share of positives truly have it?
o: About 9%
About 99%
About 50%
About 1%

panel.q: A detective is 95% sure of a suspect's guilt from evidence that is only 3 times more likely if guilty. What question should we ask?
panel.model: We should ask about the prior. A likelihood ratio of only 3 can raise belief to 95% only if the prior was already high, otherwise the confidence is too high.

panel.q: Which statement about Bayesian updating is correct?
o: Weak evidence should shift belief a little, and strong evidence more
Any piece of evidence should flip belief completely
Belief should never change once it is formed
Only experts are allowed to update their beliefs
panel.why: Updates are proportional to the likelihood ratio.

teach.model: Bayes' theorem updates belief: posterior is proportional to prior times likelihood. Base rates matter: for rare conditions most positive tests can be false alarms. The odds form multiplies prior odds by the likelihood ratio.

points.ask: What do I combine it with?
Why can a positive test mislead?

stages.title: Epistemology and justification
stages.hook: Many philosophers say knowledge is justified true belief. Can you have a justified, true belief that still is not knowledge?
explain: Epistemology is the study of knowledge: what it is, how we get it and its limits. A traditional analysis (from discussions in Plato) says knowledge is justified true belief (JTB): you believe it, it is true and you have good reasons. But Edmund Gettier (1963) gave cases where someone has a justified true belief by luck. A classic example, due to Bertrand Russell and in the same spirit: you look at a stopped clock that happens to show the correct time, and you believe the time it shows. Your belief is true and seems justified, yet it is not knowledge. Many philosophers added conditions (such as reliability or no false lemmas) and there is still no agreed analysis.

Sources of knowledge include perception, memory, testimony, reason and introspection. Empiricists stress experience; rationalists stress reasoning that does not depend on experience. Foundationalists think justification rests on basic beliefs; coherentists think beliefs justify one another in a web; reliabilists say a belief is justified if produced by a reliable process.

Fallibilism holds that we can know things without certainty, since we can be wrong. Scepticism asks whether we can know anything at all, and cases like dreaming or deception are used to test our justifications. Practical wisdom is intellectual humility: proportioning belief to evidence, and noting limits like imperfect memory, bias and expert disagreement.

example.q: You see a barn from the road and believe "That is a barn." Unknown to you, the area has many convincing fake barn fronts, and you happened to look at the one real barn. Is it knowledge?
steps: The belief is true and justified by your vision.
But you could easily have been wrong, so the success is luck.
Many philosophers say it is not knowledge.
example.a: Probably not knowledge, even though it is justified and true: the barn facade case is a Gettier-style example.

analogies.city: A friend gives you correct directions from an outdated map that happened to still be right.
analogies.tech: A calculator with a hidden bug gives a correct answer for a special case.
analogies.nature: A stopped clock is right twice a day, yet that does not make it a reliable guide.

stages.mnemonic: Believe it, true it, good reasons too, but luck can break the three-way glue.
terms: Epistemology
The philosophical study of knowledge and justified belief.
Justification
Good reasons or reliable processes supporting a belief.
Fallibilism
The view that we can know things without absolute certainty.
Empiricism
The view that knowledge comes mainly from experience.

misc.right: Most philosophers accept fallibilism: we can know without absolute certainty.

stages.limits: Epistemologists disagree about the nature of knowledge, justification and the role of luck, and about whether scepticism can be answered.

trip.prompt: Find the Gettier problem and note two proposed responses.

questions.q: What does JTB stand for?
o: Justified true belief
Judged true belief
Just the basics
Joint truth and belief
questions.why: It is the traditional analysis of knowledge.

questions.q: What did Gettier's cases show?
o: Justified true belief may not be knowledge
Knowledge is completely impossible for people
Beliefs are never true in real life
Justification is useless for knowing things
questions.why: Luck can separate JTB from knowledge.

questions.q: Empiricism says that knowledge comes mainly from...
o: Experience
Pure reason
Authority
Intuition

questions.q: Which view says beliefs justify one another in a web?
o: Coherentism
Foundationalism
Reliabilism
Empiricism

questions.q: A guess that turns out true is not knowledge mainly because...
o: It lacks justification
It turns out to be false after all
It is much too short to count as a claim
It is only an opinion held by one person
questions.why: Knowledge needs good reasons or reliability.

questions.q: Fallibilism means...
o: We can know things while admitting we could be wrong
We know nothing at all for certain
We know everything we believe
Certainty is needed before we can claim to know

questions.q: Reliabilism says a belief is justified if it...
o: Comes from a reliable process
Is popular among many different people
Is comforting to the person who holds it
Is very old and handed down for years

questions.q: Why is testimony an important source of knowledge?
o: Most of what we know we learn from others
It is always correct when people tell us
It can replace evidence in every case
It is the same as direct perception
questions.why: We rely on others, trusting reliable sources.

questions.q: Match each position to its core idea.
pairs: Beliefs support each other in a web

questions.q: A stopped clock shows the right time when you look. Explain why your belief is not knowledge.
questions.model: The clock was not a reliable source because it is stopped. My belief is true only by luck, so it is a justified true belief that is not knowledge.

panel.q: A student says "I know the exam is tomorrow", having read the wrong date by accident, and the exam is tomorrow because it was moved. Is this knowledge?
o: Probably not, since the belief is true only by luck
Yes, because it fits justified true belief
Yes, since the belief turned out to be true
Yes, as she sincerely believed it was so
panel.why: A false lemma links belief and truth.

panel.q: Why might intellectual humility be a virtue in epistemology?
panel.model: Because our knowledge is fallible, humility makes us match confidence to evidence and stay willing to revise our views.

panel.q: Which claim is a direct challenge from scepticism?
o: How do you know you are not being deceived about everything?
What is the capital city of Peru?
How fast does light travel in a vacuum?
What is the product of 7 and 8?

teach.model: Epistemology studies knowledge. Knowledge was traditionally justified true belief, but Gettier cases show luck can break it. Theories of justification include foundationalism, coherentism and reliabilism. Fallibilism says we can know without certainty.

points.ask: What is the problem with it?

stages.title: Causal inference
stages.hook: Cities with more ice cream sales also have more drownings. Does ice cream cause drowning?
explain: Correlation means two variables move together. Causation means one produces a change in the other. A correlation can arise because A causes B, B causes A, a third variable (a confounder) causes both, or by chance. Ice cream and drownings both rise in hot weather: heat is the confounder.

To infer causation we use several tools. A randomised controlled trial (RCT) assigns participants to groups at random, so on average the groups differ only by the treatment, which breaks links with confounders. When experiments are not possible, observational studies adjust for known confounders, use natural experiments, or look for features of causation: temporal order, a dose-response relationship, plausible mechanism, consistency across studies and specificity (as in Hill's considerations).

Beware of Simpson's paradox, where a trend in groups reverses when groups are combined. Causal diagrams (directed graphs) show assumed causes and help decide what to adjust for; adjusting for a collider can create false links. Counterfactual thinking defines an effect as the difference between what happened and what would have happened without the cause. Observational data can suggest causes but rarely settle them.

example.q: In a hospital study, treatment A has recovery 273/350 and B has 289/350 overall. For small stones A is 81/87 and B 234/270; for large stones A is 192/263 and B 55/80. Which looks better overall, and by group?
steps: Overall: A = 78%, B = 83%, so B looks better.
Small stones: A 93% vs B 87%, so A better.
Large stones: A 73% vs B 69%, so A better.
Reason: A was given more often to the harder large-stone cases.
example.a: B looks better overall, but A is better in each group (Simpson's paradox); case severity is a confounder.

analogies.farm: Farms that use more fertiliser may have better soil to begin with, so soil is a confounder.
analogies.sport: Players who train more may also be more motivated, so motivation confounds the link to results.
analogies.tech: Users who enable a feature may already be more active, so activity confounds the effect.

stages.mnemonic: Cause needs more than a link: rule out the third wheel, then think.
terms: Confounder
A third variable that influences both the supposed cause and the effect.
Randomised controlled trial
An experiment that assigns subjects to groups by chance.
Counterfactual
What would have happened under a different condition.
Simpson's paradox
A trend that reverses when groups are combined.

misc.wrong: If A and B are correlated, A must cause B.
misc.right: Correlation can come from reverse causation, confounders or chance.

stages.limits: Causal inference from observational data depends on assumptions that cannot be fully tested, and scholars debate methods and their limits.

trip.prompt: Find how randomisation and confounders are discussed.

questions.q: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. What is heat?
o: A confounder
A mediator only
The effect
A coincidence

questions.q: Why does randomisation help in an experiment?
o: It balances confounders between groups on average
It guarantees that the groups get equal results
It removes the effect of chance from the trial
It makes the trial shorter to run
questions.why: Groups differ only by the treatment.

questions.q: Which is NOT a way correlation can arise?
o: The variables being measured in different units
A causes B directly
A third variable causes both of them
Chance alone throws them together
questions.why: The other three are real routes.

questions.q: A study finds 273 recoveries from 350 patients on treatment A. What is the recovery rate as a decimal?
Why might it be misleading to compare raw recovery rates of two treatments given to different types of patients?
o: Severity may confound the comparison
Treatments never differ between patients
Recovery rates are always equal in groups
Patients simply dislike some treatments

questions.q: Dose-response evidence supports causation because...
o: More exposure giving a larger effect is expected if there is a causal link
Doses are expensive to give out
It proves the whole mechanism in full
It removes every kind of bias
questions.why: It is one of Hill's considerations.

questions.q: A counterfactual effect is...
o: The difference between what happened and what would have happened without the cause
The sum of all the causes of an event
A correlation seen between two variables
An opinion about what might have happened
questions.why: It compares with the unobserved scenario.

questions.q: Match each idea to its meaning.
pairs: The effect actually causes the supposed cause

questions.q: Put the steps for assessing a causal claim in order.
items: Think of alternative explanations such as confounders
Look for experimental or natural-experiment evidence
Judge how strongly the evidence supports causation

questions.q: People who carry lighters get lung cancer more often. Does carrying a lighter cause cancer? Explain.
questions.model: No, smoking is a confounder: smokers carry lighters and smoking causes lung cancer, so the lighter is only associated with cancer.

panel.q: Why is it hard to run a randomised trial on whether smoking causes cancer in humans?
o: It would be unethical to assign people to smoke
Smoking is illegal in many places
Cancer is far too rare to study
Trials are always biased in some way
panel.why: Ethics limits experiments, so observational evidence was used.

panel.q: Explain how Simpson's paradox can make a treatment look worse overall although it is better in every subgroup.
panel.model: If the better treatment is given more often to harder cases, the combined rate is dragged down, so the overall comparison reverses even though it wins in each group; the case mix is a confounder.

panel.q: Which design gives the strongest evidence of a causal effect?
o: A well-run randomised controlled trial
A single anecdote from one person
A survey that has no comparison group
An expert's strong hunch about the cause

teach.model: Correlation is not causation: a link may come from cause, reverse cause, a confounder or chance. Randomised trials balance confounders. Observational studies need careful adjustment and several kinds of supporting evidence. Beware of Simpson's paradox.

points.ask: What is the best way to test a cause?

stages.title: Advanced critical thinking
stages.hook: A study of 20 outcomes finds one "significant" result at p < 0.05 and the headline says "Breakthrough!". Should you be impressed?
explain: Advanced critical thinking applies careful tests to evidence in complex settings. Statistical significance (a small p-value) means data as extreme as observed would be unusual if there were no effect. It does not tell you the probability the hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about size or importance.

Watch for common traps. Multiple comparisons: test 20 independent null effects at the 5% level and the chance of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.95^20 ≈ 64%. Publication bias: studies with exciting results are more often published. Survivorship bias: we look only at what survived, like successful companies, and miss the failures. Regression to the mean: extreme results tend to be followed by less extreme ones, so a "cure" after a bad week may be nothing. Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure.

The replication crisis in some fields showed that many published results do not hold up on repetition, which led to better practice such as pre-registration, larger samples and open data. A mature critical thinker asks: what is the effect size and its uncertainty, what are the alternatives, who funded it, and has it been independently replicated? Healthy scepticism is calibrated, not blanket doubt.

example.q: You test 10 independent hypotheses that are all false, each at the 5% level. What is the chance at least one looks significant?
steps: P(none significant) = 0.95^10.
At least one: 1 − 0.599 ≈ 0.401.

analogies.city: A school ranks "improvement" on test scores; teachers teach to the test, so scores rise while learning does not (Goodhart).
analogies.sport: The best rookie of the year often does worse the next year because part of the first performance was luck (regression to the mean).
analogies.tech: A company lists successful startups that dropped out of university but ignores the many that failed (survivorship).

stages.mnemonic: Ask: how many tried, who is missing, what is the size, can it repeat?
terms: p-value
The probability of data this extreme if there were no real effect.
Publication bias
A tendency to publish only exciting or positive results.
Survivorship bias
Judging from the survivors while ignoring those that did not survive.
Goodhart's law
A measure that becomes a target ceases to be a good measure.

misc.wrong: A p-value below 0.05 means the hypothesis is 95% likely to be true.
misc.right: The p-value is the chance of such data if there were no effect, not the chance the hypothesis is true.

stages.limits: Experts argue about the best use of p-values, and no single rule replaces judgment about the quality of a study.

trip.prompt: Find the factors blamed for non-replicable results.

The hypothesis is therefore certainly true
The effect found is large and important
The study was carried out perfectly
questions.why: It is about the data under the null.

All studies are published, whatever they find
Journals simply invent data to fill the pages
Results vanish by themselves over time
questions.why: Published studies are a biased sample.

Anchoring on the first fund seen
Hindsight, from looking back at past results
Framing, from how the returns are shown

o: Regression to the mean
A curse that follows great players
Bad luck only, and nothing else at all
A change in the rules of the game
questions.why: Part of extreme performance is chance.

questions.q: A hospital is judged on waiting-time targets and staff move patients to hit the numbers. This is...
o: Goodhart's law
Survivorship bias
Confirmation bias
Simpson's paradox

questions.q: Why is effect size important along with significance?
o: A tiny effect can be significant with a huge sample
Significance is the same as size
Effect size is always large in a study
It matters only in medicine and nowhere else
questions.why: Importance is not the same as significance.

questions.q: Match each problem to its description.
pairs: Many tests raise the chance of false positives
Extreme results tend to become less extreme
Ignoring those that did not survive

questions.q: Put the steps in order when you see a striking study result.
items: Check the sample size and design
Ask how many comparisons were made
Look at effect size and uncertainty

questions.q: Explain why a single study with a surprising result should not be taken as settled.
questions.model: A surprising result may be a fluke or have bias, so it needs independent replication before we rely on it.

panel.q: A drug trial reports 20 outcomes and highlights the one that was significant. What should you ask?
o: How many outcomes were tested and were they pre-specified?
What colour is the drug that was used?
Who is the author of the paper?
How long is the paper in total?

panel.q: Why does survivorship bias make success stories misleading?
panel.model: We see only the successes, not the many who did the same and failed, so the sample is biased and may reflect luck rather than a good strategy.
panel.why: Missing failures hide the real odds.

panel.q: What is the best attitude to scientific claims?
o: Proportion belief to the quality and replication of the evidence
Reject all science as untrustworthy
Accept every headline you read
Trust only your own gut feeling

teach.model: Look beyond a headline. P-values are not the chance a hypothesis is true. Many tests inflate false positives. Watch for publication bias, survivorship bias, regression to the mean and Goodhart's law. Ask about effect size, uncertainty and replication.

points.ask: What if many tests are run?

stages.title: Strategic optimisation
stages.hook: You have 4 hours to split between studying maths and writing an essay. How do you decide how to split the time?
explain: Optimisation is choosing the best option under constraints. It needs an objective (what to maximise or minimise), decision variables (what you control) and constraints (limits). Resources are scarce, so every choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative you give up.

Marginal analysis asks whether the next unit of effort adds more benefit than cost. Keep adding while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost. Often returns diminish: the first hour of study helps more than the fifth. In simple linear problems the best answer lies at a corner of the feasible region. For example, maximise profit 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4 and x ≤ 3 (x, y ≥ 0). Corners: (0,0)=0, (3,0)=9, (3,1)=11, (0,4)=8. The maximum is 11 at (3, 1).

Beware of optimising the wrong thing, of local optima (a peak that is not the highest), and of fragile optimum solutions that fail if conditions shift. Satisficing means accepting a solution that is good enough, which is rational when searching is costly. A Pareto improvement makes someone better off without making anyone worse off; a Pareto-optimal state has no such improvement. Robust strategies often beat narrowly optimal ones in an uncertain world.

example.q: Maximise 3x + 2y with x + y ≤ 4, x ≤ 3, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Find the best (x, y).
steps: List the corners of the feasible region: (0,0), (3,0), (3,1), (0,4).
The largest is 11 at (3,1).

analogies.farm: A farmer splits land between two crops to maximise profit given water and labour limits.
analogies.sport: A coach has limited training time and spreads it over skills where improvement per hour is greatest.
analogies.home: You choose how to spend a weekly budget so that the last coin spent gives about equal benefit everywhere.

Constraint

Opportunity cost
The value of the best alternative given up.
Pareto optimal

misc.right: The best choice depends on assumptions. If they change, the optimum may change.

stages.limits: Optimisation requires a clear objective, but real goals are often several and conflicting, and weights on them are a matter of values.

trip.prompt: Find the terms objective function and constraints.

Why might a robust but slightly worse plan beat a narrowly optimal one?
questions.model: The narrowly optimal plan may depend on assumptions that could change and fail badly, while a robust plan still does well across conditions.

panel.q: Maximise 2x + 3y with x + y ≤ 5, y ≤ 4, x, y ≥ 0. Corners: (0,0), (5,0), (1,4), (0,4). What is the best?
o: (1,4) with value 14
(5,0) with value 10
(0,4) with value 12
(0,0) with value 0

panel.q: Explain why spending an extra hour on a task you have almost perfected may be a poor choice.
panel.model: Returns diminish, so the marginal benefit is small, and the hour could give more value elsewhere (opportunity cost).

teach.model: Optimisation chooses the best option given an objective and constraints. Compare marginal benefit and cost, remember opportunity cost and diminishing returns, and in linear problems check the corners of the feasible region. A robust, good-enough plan can beat a fragile optimum.

stages.title: Risk and uncertainty analysis
stages.hook: A "1-in-100-year" flood happened last year. Does that mean it cannot happen again for 99 years?
explain: Risk combines how likely a harmful event is with how bad it would be. A simple measure is expected loss = probability × impact. A 2% chance of losing 10,000 has expected loss 200, equal to a 100% chance of losing 200 in size, although the experiences are very different. Risk matrices and registers rank risks by likelihood and impact.

A "1-in-100-year" event has a 1% chance in any given year, independent of the last one. Over 10 years the chance of at least one is 1 − 0.99^10 ≈ 9.6%. Over 100 years it is about 63%. Risk analysis distinguishes risk (known probabilities), uncertainty (unknown probabilities) and "unknown unknowns". Tail risks are rare events with huge impact, which averages can hide; fat-tailed distributions make extreme events far more likely than a bell curve suggests.

Managing risk means avoiding, reducing, transferring (like insurance), or accepting it. Precaution should be proportionate: consider the cost of protection, irreversibility, and the quality of evidence. People misjudge risk through availability, dread and optimism, and communicating risk is clearer with natural frequencies ("1 in 100") and absolute rather than only relative numbers. A premortem, imagining the project has failed and asking why, reveals risks early.

example.q: A warehouse has a 2% yearly chance of a 50,000 loss and a 20% chance of a 2,000 loss. Which has the higher expected annual loss?
steps: The first is higher.
example.a: The rare large loss: 1,000 versus 400 per year.

analogies.farm: A farmer buys crop insurance to transfer the risk of drought.
analogies.city: A city builds flood defences for rare but severe floods.
analogies.tech: A company backs up data to reduce the impact of a failure.

stages.mnemonic: Chance times cost sets the size; tails and the unknown ask for margin.
terms: Risk
The combination of the likelihood and impact of a harmful event.
Expected loss
Probability multiplied by the size of the loss.
Tail risk
A rare event with very large impact.
Premortem
Imagining failure in advance to find causes.

misc.wrong: After a 1-in-100-year flood, the next one is 100 years away.
misc.right: Each year has about a 1% chance regardless of the past.

stages.limits: Probabilities of rare events are hard to estimate, so risk numbers often hide deep uncertainty.

trip.prompt: Find the difference between risk and uncertainty.

questions.q: A "1-in-100-year" event has a 1% chance per year. What is the probability of at least one in 10 years? Give a decimal to three places.
A 5% chance of a 4,000 loss has what expected loss?
What does a risk matrix compare?
o: Likelihood and impact
Cost and price of the project
Speed and size of the team
Time and place of the event
questions.why: It ranks risks on two axes.

questions.q: A tail risk is...
o: A rare event with huge impact
A frequent event with small impact
An event that is perfectly safe
A rough estimate of a likely cost

questions.q: Insurance is an example of...
o: Transferring risk
Avoiding the risk completely
Accepting the risk as it is
Ignoring the risk and hoping for the best
questions.why: The risk shifts to the insurer.

questions.q: Why is "1 in 100" often clearer than "1%" for the public?
o: Natural frequencies are easier to grasp
They are more accurate than percentages
They are shorter to write down
They sound more scientific to readers

questions.q: A premortem helps because it...
o: Reveals why a plan might fail before it does
Replaces the need for any planning
Blames particular people for the failure
Predicts the future exactly as it will be

questions.q: Which is uncertainty rather than risk?
o: Probabilities that nobody can estimate
A fair die roll with known chances
A coin toss with equal odds
A lottery with published odds

questions.q: Match each response to the risk strategy.
Explain why expected loss can be a misleading guide for rare catastrophic events.
questions.model: The average hides that a rare event can be so severe it cannot be recovered from, and its probability is hard to estimate, so we may need extra protection beyond the expected value.

panel.q: A project has a 10% chance of failure each year, independent each year. What is the chance of surviving 3 years without failure?
o: About 73%
About 90%
About 80%
About 30%

panel.q: Why might a precautionary approach be sensible when an outcome is irreversible?
panel.model: Because a mistake cannot be undone, it can be worth paying for protection or waiting for more evidence before acting.
panel.why: Irreversibility raises the cost of error.

panel.q: Which is the best use of a risk register?
o: Track risks, their likelihood, impact and owners, and update it
File it once and never look at it again
Hide the risks from the people involved
Use it to replace all decisions

teach.model: Risk is likelihood combined with impact. Expected loss is probability times size, but tail risks and irreversible harms need extra care. A 1-in-100-year event has a 1% chance each year. Manage risk by avoiding, reducing, transferring or accepting it, and use premortems.

stages.title: Negotiation and conflict resolution
stages.hook: Two neighbours both want the same room in a shared house. One says "I need it for study." The other says "I need it for my music." What might they do?
explain: Negotiation is a process in which parties with some shared and some opposed interests try to reach an agreement. In principled negotiation (Fisher and Ury), you separate the people from the problem, focus on interests rather than positions, invent options for mutual gain, and use objective criteria. A position is what you say you want ("the big room"); an interest is why ("quiet to study").

Key concepts: your BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) is what you will do if no deal is reached; it sets your walk-away point. The zone of possible agreement (ZOPA) is the range where a deal can satisfy both sides: if a seller will accept at least 90 and a buyer will pay at most 120, the ZOPA is 90 to 120. Many negotiations are not zero-sum: trading what you value less for what you value more creates value (integrative bargaining). Distributive bargaining just divides a fixed amount.

Conflict resolution adds listening, acknowledging feelings, and fair processes such as mediation, where a neutral person helps the parties, or arbitration, where a neutral decides. Anchoring effects, escalation and loss of face can block agreements. Cultural norms about directness and time differ, so no single style is superior. Ethical negotiation means honesty about what you say; bluffing about facts harms trust, especially in repeated relationships.

example.q: A seller will accept no less than 90. A buyer will pay no more than 120. They settle at the midpoint. What price?
steps: ZOPA: 90 to 120.
Each gains 15 over their walk-away.

analogies.home: Siblings share a chore chart by trading jobs each prefers.
analogies.farm: Two farmers agree one grazes in the dry season and the other in the wet.
analogies.city: A tenant and landlord compromise on rent and repairs.

stages.mnemonic: Interests not positions; options for both; BATNA is your door.
terms: BATNA
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement; your fallback.
Interest
The underlying reason behind a position.
ZOPA
The range where both sides can accept a deal.
Mediation
A neutral helper guides the parties towards agreement.

misc.wrong: Negotiation is a contest in which one side must lose.
misc.right: Many negotiations have options that benefit both sides, especially when parties value things differently.

stages.limits: Negotiation advice is drawn from particular settings, and power differences and cultural norms can limit what works.

A fixed price put on the deal

o: It increases

o: Split it by use so both get what they need

pairs: Creating value by trading what each values differently

questions.q: Put the steps of principled negotiation in order.
Explain why focusing on interests rather than positions can lead to better agreements.
questions.model: Different positions may hide compatible interests, so understanding why each side wants something opens more creative options that satisfy both.

panel.q: A negotiator reveals her BATNA is very weak. What is the likely effect?
o: The other side may press for better terms
She gains more power at the table
Nothing changes in the talks
The deal becomes certain to happen

panel.q: Why might using objective criteria, such as market prices, help in a dispute?
panel.model: Objective standards give a fair basis that both sides can accept, so the outcome depends on reasons rather than pressure or willpower.

panel.q: Cultures differ in negotiating style, such as directness. What is a wise approach?
o: Learn the other side's norms and avoid assuming yours are the only ones
Insist on your own style at the table
Ignore culture, because it does not matter

teach.model: Negotiate on interests, not positions. Know your BATNA and the zone of possible agreement. Look for options that create value for both sides and use objective criteria. Mediation can help when talks stall. Honesty protects trust.

stages.title: Complex problem-solving
stages.hook: How would you approach a problem like reducing a city's traffic when every fix seems to cause a new problem?
explain: Complex problems have many interacting parts, unclear goals, uncertainty and no single right answer. Rittel and Webber called such open-ended social problems "wicked problems": they cannot be fully defined in advance, solutions are not simply true or false, and every attempt changes the problem.

A useful approach is iterative. Frame the problem and test the framing; gather evidence from several viewpoints; break the problem into parts but keep sight of the whole and the links between parts; build simple models; generate options; test small, learn from feedback; and adapt. Tools include system maps, decision trees, scenario planning, premortems and red teams (people assigned to find weaknesses). Experts solve problems partly by recognising patterns from experience, but they can also be overconfident, so check against evidence.

Common traps are jumping to a solution, solving the wrong problem, tunnel vision on one factor, ignoring side effects, and sticking with a plan after it stops working. Good practice is to state assumptions, seek disconfirming evidence, set review points, and combine different kinds of knowledge, including from people affected. Knowledge transfer, applying ideas from one field to another, happens best when you understand the deep structure of a problem, not only its surface features.

example.q: A town wants to cut flooding. List a sensible iterative approach in four moves.
steps: Frame: find causes (rainfall, drainage, building on flood plains).
Model and options: map the system, list options such as drains, green space and zoning.
Test small: pilot in one district; measure results.
Review and adapt: scale what works and revise what does not.
example.a: Frame, model, pilot and adapt, with several viewpoints and review points.

analogies.city: Planning a bus network involves riders, costs, traffic, and many trade-offs.
analogies.farm: Changing crops affects soil, water, markets and workers at once.
analogies.tech: Building a large app requires modules, testing and user feedback in cycles.

stages.mnemonic: Frame, map, try small, learn, adapt: the loop for a tangled knot.
terms: Wicked problem
A complex social problem with no clear definition or single right solution.
Red team
A group that challenges a plan to expose weaknesses.
Iteration
Repeating a cycle of try, learn and improve.
Transfer
Applying knowledge from one situation to a new one.

misc.wrong: A hard problem needs one clever idea.
misc.right: Complex problems usually need several steps, many viewpoints and repeated adjustment.

stages.limits: Frameworks for complex problem-solving are guides, not guarantees, and evidence on what works varies by field.

Why is iteration better than a single big plan for a complex problem?
questions.model: Complex problems are uncertain and respond unpredictably, so testing small steps and learning from feedback lets us adapt instead of committing to a plan that may be wrong.

panel.q: A team starts building a solution before agreeing on what the problem is. What is the likely risk?
o: They solve the wrong problem
They finish the project early
They learn a great deal about bias
They avoid every kind of bias

panel.q: How can you reduce overconfidence in a plan?
panel.model: Run a premortem or red team, state assumptions, and seek evidence that could show the plan is wrong, with review points to check progress.

panel.q: Which approach best fits a wicked problem?
o: Iterate with feedback, several viewpoints and small tests
Find one perfect solution first and then apply it
Ignore the stakeholders who disagree
Fix the plan permanently and do not change it

teach.model: Complex problems have interacting parts, uncertainty and no single answer. Frame the problem, gather several viewpoints, model the system, test small and learn from feedback. Use premortems and red teams to challenge your plan.
